rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Predict the products formed when \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\) reacts with the following reagents : (Any two)
(i) \(\mathrm{PhMgBr}\) and then \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{HCN}\)
rows.solution:
(i) WITH PHENYLMAGNESIUM BROMIDE, then acid. The Grignard reagent adds its phenyl group to the carbonyl carbon, and hydrolysis gives the alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr}} \mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH(OH){-}CH_2CH_3}\)

The product is 1-PHENYLPROPAN-1-OL, a SECONDARY alcohol — as an aldehyde other than methanal always gives, its carbonyl carbon ending up bonded to one hydrogen and two carbons.

(ii) WITH LITHIUM ALUMINIUM HYDRIDE. The hydride delivers \(\mathrm{H^-}\) to the carbonyl carbon and the aldehyde is reduced to a PRIMARY alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\)

The product is PROPAN-1-OL. Sodium borohydride would serve equally well and is the gentler reagent.

(iii) WITH HYDROGEN CYANIDE. Cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon and a proton to the oxygen, giving the CYANOHYDRIN:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(OH)CN}\)

The product is 2-HYDROXYBUTANENITRILE, with FOUR carbons where the aldehyde had three — the cyanide has added one. Cyanohydrins are useful precisely for that: hydrolysing the nitrile gives a hydroxy acid.

rows.stem: Define molar conductivity for the solution of an electrolyte. How does it vary with concentration ?
rows.solution:
MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY is the conducting power of ALL the ions furnished by ONE MOLE of an electrolyte in solution. Formally it is the conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole, held between two electrodes one centimetre apart:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{\mathrm{C}} = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{\mathrm{C\ in\ mol\ L^{-1}}}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The factor of 1000 converts litres to cubic centimetres, \(\kappa\) being per centimetre while the concentration is per litre.

HOW IT VARIES: molar conductivity INCREASES on DILUTION, for every electrolyte — but the two classes behave differently, and the difference identifies them.

A STRONG electrolyte is fully dissociated at every concentration, so the number of ions from one mole does not change. The rise on dilution is GRADUAL, and comes only from the ions moving further apart and interfering with one another's migration less. A plot against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is a straight line, and extrapolating it gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\).

A WEAK electrolyte is only partly ionised, and dilution shifts that equilibrium towards MORE ions, so one mole furnishes more of them. The rise is STEEP, steepest of all near infinite dilution, and the curve never meets the axis — so its \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) must come from Kohlrausch's law instead.

Note that CONDUCTIVITY, measured for a fixed VOLUME, moves the OPPOSITE way and falls on dilution.

rows.stem: In a reaction \(2\mathrm{N_2O_5\,(g)} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{NO_2\,(g)} + \mathrm{O_2\,(g)}\), the concentration of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) decreases from \(0{\cdot}5\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) to \(0{\cdot}4\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) in 10 minutes. Calculate the average rate of this reaction and rate of production of \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) during this period.
rows.solution:
The AVERAGE RATE is one number for the whole reaction, obtained by dividing each species' own rate by its coefficient:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{O_2}]}{\Delta t}\)

The concentration of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) falls by \(0{\cdot}5 - 0{\cdot}4 = 0{\cdot}1\) mol per litre in 10 minutes:
\(\text{Rate} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{10}\)

\(\text{Rate} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ min^{-1}}\)

RATE OF PRODUCTION OF \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) — its coefficient is 4, so it appears at FOUR TIMES the rate of reaction:
\(\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{\Delta t} = 4 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(= 2 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ min^{-1}}\)

The division by 2 and the multiplication by 4 are the whole content of the question: without them the same reaction would have three different "rates" depending on which species was watched.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the equations involved in the following reactions :
(i) Cannizzaro reaction
(ii) Aldol condensation
(iii) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction
rows.solution:
(i) CANNIZZARO REACTION — a disproportionation of an aldehyde having NO \(\alpha\) hydrogen, treated with concentrated alkali. One molecule is oxidised and another reduced:
\(2\,\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{NaOH\ (conc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOONa}\)

Benzaldehyde behaves the same way, giving benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate. The absence of an \(\alpha\) hydrogen is what makes this route available.

(ii) ALDOL CONDENSATION — requires an aldehyde or ketone that DOES have an \(\alpha\) hydrogen. The enolate of one molecule attacks the carbonyl carbon of another, and the aldol so formed loses water on warming:
\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH{-}CHO} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The dehydration happens readily because the new double bond is CONJUGATED with the carbonyl.

(iii) HELL-VOLHARD-ZELINSKY REACTION halogenates a carboxylic acid at its \(\alpha\) position, with a little red phosphorus as catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}\)

The phosphorus is essential: it converts the acid into its acyl halide, which enolises far more readily than the acid itself, and it is the enol that the halogen attacks. Formic acid does not respond, having no \(\alpha\) carbon at all.

rows.stem:
(i) Which acid of each pair would you expect to be stronger ? Give reason.
(I) \(\mathrm{F-CH_2-COOH}\) or \(\mathrm{Cl-CH_2-COOH}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\) or \(\mathrm{p-O_2N-C_6H_4-COOH}\)
(ii) Distinguish between Propanal and Propanone.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — In sub-part (i) the pair (II) is printed as two DRAWN STRUCTURES side by side, separated by the word 'or': a benzene ring (hexagon with three Kekule double bonds, NOT an inner circle) bearing COOH on the top vertex, and a second identical ring bearing COOH on the top vertex and NO2 on the bottom (para) vertex. Pair (I) is printed as linear formulas, not drawings. The stem gives each drawn compound its name in formula form - benzoic acid and 4-nitrobenzoic acid - which is a lossless reading that does NOT hand over the answer, since the question is which is the stronger acid and that still requires the -I effect of NO2 (the marking scheme answers 'p-nitrobenzoic acid, due to -I effect of NO2 group'). Classified ILLUSTRATIVE rather than REQUIRED for that reason: the row is fully answerable from the stem text. The crop is still worth attaching so the page is reproduced. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) FLUOROACETIC ACID is the stronger.

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the anion left behind, and anything that WITHDRAWS electron density spreads the carboxylate's charge and stabilises it. FLUORINE is more electronegative than chlorine, so its \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect is stronger and it withdraws more. The \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) values are 2.59 against chloroacetic acid's 2.86.

(I I) 4-NITROBENZOIC ACID is the stronger.

The NITRO group withdraws electron density both inductively and by RESONANCE, and from the PARA position its resonance reaches the carboxyl group directly. The anion is therefore more stable than benzoate, and the acid stronger — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 3.44 against benzoic acid's 4.19.

The same substituent at the para position of a phenol acts the same way, which is why 4-nitrophenol is far more acidic than phenol.

(ii) Use TOLLENS' REAGENT. Warmed with it, PROPANAL gives a bright SILVER MIRROR, the aldehyde being oxidised to propanoic acid while silver ion is reduced to the metal; PROPANONE gives no reaction, a ketone resisting such mild oxidation.

Fehling's solution serves the same way, propanal giving a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.

The IODOFORM TEST would also distinguish them, but in the OPPOSITE direction: propanone carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group and gives the yellow precipitate, while propanal — \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\) — does not. Either test serves, provided the direction is stated correctly.
